newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany to meet 3.0 pct deficit-govt sources.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany to meet 3.0 pct deficit-govt sources.

text.p: Government sources on Thursday said Germany would meet the deficit target for a single European currency of 3.0 percent of economic output in 1997 although the federal deficit is projected to balloon to 71.2 billion marks ($40.4 billion).
Total public sector debt will be slightly over the target of 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the sources said, but will be brought back into line by 2001.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel is due to present to the cabinet on Friday a draft budget for 1998, as well as a supplementary budget for 1997 showing a federal deficit up from 53.3 billion marks in the original plan.
To do so, the constitution requires him to declare that the economy is out of balance if the deficit exceeds government investment.

Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) budget spokesman Karl Diller attacked Waigel's budget plans, saying Bonn had abandoned its goals of fighting joblessness and pushed higher debt burdens onto future generations.
Diller told journalists Waigel had no grounds to exceed constitutional limits with the higher 1997 deficit.

"The principle of a sustainable security in state finances has been thrown overboard and burdens have just been postponed for the future," Diller said. "Waigel's bridge to 1999 does not rest on a secure bank, it hovers above the abyss."

But the government sources said "positive developments in federal special assets and social security" would help offset the larger federal deficit and help meet the deficit target for European monetary union. They gave no details.

In its long-term financial plan, the government sees growth rates as moderate but steady, the sources said. GDP growth in 1997 is seen at 2.5 percent, rising to 2.75 percent next year and coming back to 2.5 percent in each of the three years following.

The 1997 supplementary budget foresees a deficit of 71.2 billion marks, up from 53.3 billion in the original plan. In 1998, the deficit is expected to fall back to 57.8 billion marks. Privatisation revenues in 1998 are seen rising to 19.7 billion marks from 12.7 billion this year.
Although the SPD had demanded since February that Waigel present a supplementary budget, Diller said the plan Waigel has come up with did too little to create jobs.
It also forces Waigel to declare that the government has lost its grip on the economic balance, as the constitution requires if the deficit exceeds government investment.
"There are no conceptual grounds (for such a declaration) in this supplementary budget," Diller said.

The SPD will oppose the government's plans to cut the solidarity income tax surcharge, raised to help rebuild ex-communist eastern Germany, since they would force states to give up 3.5 billion marks in revenue.
The coalition's tax reform plans, now being debated in parliament's mediation committee, would cut revenues by about 20 billion marks a year, placing additional pressures on the deficit, Diller said.
Its pension reform plans would cost another 15 billion marks a year.
